QuestionStmt.S: Let $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 2k-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2k-1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2k-1 \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2k-1 & 1 \\ 1-2k & 0 & k \\ -1 & -k & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ where $k$ is a real number. If $$\det(\text{adj } A) + \det(\text{adj } B) = 11^6,$$ then the value of $k - 5$ is equal to

Solution.S:
Step 1: For a square matrix of order $n$, we have $\det(\text{adj } X) = (\det X)^{n-1}$.

Here both matrices are of order $3$, so

$$\det(\text{adj } A) = (\det A)^2$$

and

$$\det(\text{adj } B) = (\det B)^2.$$

Step 2: Matrix $A$ is upper triangular, so its determinant is the product of its diagonal elements.

$$A = \begin{bmatrix} 2k-1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2k-1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2k-1 \end{bmatrix}$$

Thus,

$$\det A = (2k-1)^3.$$

Hence,

$$\det(\text{adj } A) = \{(2k-1)^3\}^2 = (2k-1)^6.$$

Step 3: Matrix $B$ is skew-symmetric (since $B^T = -B$).

For a skew-symmetric matrix of odd order, the determinant is always zero.

$$B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2k-1 & 1 \\ 1-2k & 0 & k \\ -1 & -k & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$

So,

$$\det B = 0.$$

Therefore,

$$\det(\text{adj } B) = (\det B)^2 = 0.$$

Step 4: Given that $\det(\text{adj } A) + \det(\text{adj } B) = 11^6$,

we get

$$(2k-1)^6 + 0 = 11^6.$$

Thus,

$$(2k-1)^6 = 11^6.$$

Taking the sixth root on both sides:

$$2k-1 = \pm 11.$$

So,

$$2k-1 = 11 \Rightarrow k = 6$$

or

$$2k-1 = -11 \Rightarrow k = -5.$$

Step 5: Since the options contain $k-5$, we check $k=6$:

$$k-5 = 6 - 5 = 1.$$

Final Answer: $$\boxed{1}$$

Hence, the correct option is A.
